# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send the owner's instructions for how the agent works to `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md` (`toolkit rule add`), never to memory. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Write only a general selection rule, as a rule with `toolkit rule add`, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Owner Preferences

How the owner wants the agent to work in this project. Follow every line, every session. Each line ends with the date and where the instruction came from. Change this file only with `toolkit rule add` or `toolkit rule update`, after the owner says so.

## Git

- Keep commit messages under 50 characters. (2026-09-29, Mike Rihm, in chat)

## Replies

- Always show status as a table. (2026-09-29, Mike Rihm, in chat)
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Work finish

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Takes an approved item through the pull request, merge, deployment, and requirements update to Done, or cancels it; it never marks Done without the owner's approval and never runs a production deploy. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Check the result approval is recorded. Not recorded: when the history shows no `acceptance-checker` check of this result since its last build, run `work-check` first, which starts it (it runs whoever built the change; the result approval and the finish are refused without it). Then show the result, the gaps, and the evidence, and ask. "Ship it" or "mark it done" after he saw the result counts: save his words first, then record it (`references/approvals.md`, section 4). Each sub-item needs its own.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
2. Repository work: commit the item's files by name on its branch, push it, open the pull request, and set the stage (`references/closing.md`, section 2; `references/git-rules.md` before any Git write).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
3. Merge through `merge-and-clean-up` only with the owner's yes to this merge, or a standing merge instruction with an independent check on the exact head (`references/closing.md`, section 3). No remote: the local merge (`references/closing.md`, section 4), then this note.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'No remote: merged locally into <default branch>.' --effect 'No pull request; no deployment.'`
4. Deployment, when the item needs one (`references/closing.md`, section 5). Production deploys and production data loads are the owner's to run. Salesforce: a sandbox validate runs; a sandbox deploy needs his yes for that deploy, and in Codex he runs every sandbox deploy and sandbox data change himself, so give him the exact command with its `-o <sandbox>`. Run each `sf` command directly, never from a script.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 13-deployment`
5. Requirements baseline: copy only delivered and approved behavior into the area's file in `requirements/`, update `system-guide/` when the structure changed, and save both with `publish-docs` (`references/closing.md`, section 6).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 14-spec-update`
6. Sub-items: list the open ones; each is finished, cancelled, or moved on its own (`references/closing.md`, section 7).
   `toolkit work list --tree`
7. Memory: at most one `event` record through `memory-save`, only when the episode will matter later.
8. Before Done, run the Done checklist in `references/approvals.md`, section 5, with the Overview and Roadmap updates and the leftover worktrees in `references/closing.md`, sections 9 and 10. Take the item off the current focus now, before the finish command, so the backup it makes holds the new focus (`references/current-focus.md`); if the finish refuses, put the item back. Then mark it Done. The command also backs up the tracker and memory: read its backup line. "No backup folder is set" or a line with "failed" goes to the owner as a question (`references/closing.md`, section 10).
   `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'`
9. Say whether the work reached the default branch. End with the one question (the merge, the deploy, a leftover branch, the backup folder) or "Tell me the next thing to build."
10. Cancel instead: the owner's words are the reason; ask about each open sub-item first (`references/approvals.md`, section 6).
    `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Never mark Done without a recorded result approval or the owner's quoted words. The CLI needs `--by`, and `--quote` when no result approval is recorded.
- Never mark Done while the item's changes, or its `requirements/` and `system-guide/` updates, are uncommitted.
- A result approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Each needs the owner's yes or a standing instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md`.
- A standing merge instruction needs an `acceptance-checker` that did not build the change to find no blocking issue on that exact head. Without that check, ask the owner.
- Agents never run a production deploy or a production data load. Hand the owner the exact command and what to check afterwards; record his report in a history note.
- In Codex, every Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`references/git-rules.md`). No remote: never run `git fetch` or `git push`.
- No AI credit in commits, pull requests, or release notes. The pull request description goes through `unslop`.
- Stages that do not apply are skipped, each with one history note saying so.
- Leave the folder or card where it is. Moving or archiving is `work-organize`'s, on the owner's request.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Close the issue as completed, or as not planned for a cancel (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): the independent check of the exact head before a merge under a standing merge instruction. Brief it as `work-check` does and name the commit (`references/helpers.md`).
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. Only when this host cannot start a worker (no `spawn_agent` tool) do the work yourself, and say that no independent check ran. The `acceptance-checker` still runs when the owner chose owner-led delivery or no agent team. Without an independent check, a standing merge instruction does not apply: ask the owner.

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Walks the owner through what waits on him, one decision at a time, and records each answer where it belongs. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Build the queue. The command lists each decision once: requirements waiting for approval, proposed designs, results at stage 11, Open Questions rows the owner decides, and memory proposals. Its "Agent to-do" lines are not decisions. A delivery offer belongs to `work-delegate`: open it after his other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. He gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision; when two could match, ask which, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" with no question asked is not an answer (`references/approvals.md`, section 1).
3. Otherwise start with the count and one short line for every waiting decision, memory proposals included ("3 decisions wait on you: the WI-004 design, the WI-006 result, and a memory proposal about deploy days."). Then take them one at a time, the one blocking the most work first: what is decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. One decision per message, in the reply text.
4. An approval: read the item, then run that gate's checklist in `references/approvals.md` (requirements: section 2; design: section 3; result: section 4). A result with no independent acceptance check since its last build (the command prints a note): open `work-check` first, which runs it whoever built the change.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
5. An Open Questions answer: save his words first, rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and Answered, then set `waiting_on` back (`references/recording-owner-answers.md`, sections 4 and 5).
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line, and when it names a concept, the concept it would join. Recommend a yes only with evidence from this project (what he said, what happened, and when); with none, ask without a recommendation. Yes: approve it (a proposal for a concept is then added to it as a section). A proposal that names no concept: name the concept it goes in with `--concept`, an existing one of its type or a new key named for its subject, never for the fact (`references/proposals.md`, "Recording the owner's answer"). No: reject it, and never propose the same fact again.
   `toolkit memory list --type <type>`
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner> --concept <type>_<subject> --title '<Concept title>' --description '<one-line summary of the concept>'`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add the row inside the `publish-docs` save workspace, in the order in `references/decisions-log.md`.
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. Update the current focus when an answer changed an item's next step (`references/current-focus.md`). After each recorded answer, list the decisions again and name what still waits on him, memory proposals included, by name ("One decision still waits: the memory proposal about Ghost slugs."). A decision an earlier reply said you would take next is taken next. Empty queue: say so and offer `work-on` for unblocked items. End with the next decision's question or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work decisions`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue. A bare question is not enough. The one exception is a memory proposal with no evidence from this project (step 6).
- Ask in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for it Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit those rows again by hand.

# The current focus

Purpose: the format of the current focus, when to change it, and the exact
read-change-save sequence, in every memory backend.

## Contents

- What the focus is for
- The format
- What goes in each section
- When to check it
- Read, change, save
- A new project's focus
- Examples
- Checklist for a focus save

## What the focus is for

The current focus is the first thing the next session reads: the session
briefing includes it. It says what is happening now and where the next
session starts. It never repeats the tracker: a work item's status, tasks,
and history stay in the work item.

| Backend | Where the focus lives |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in | `.memory/CURRENT_FOCUS.md` in the main checkout |
| Hindsight | The document `focus` in the project's bank |
| Notion | The "Current focus" page under the project's page |

The same commands read and save it in every backend. Never edit the file or
the page by hand.

## The format

The model's format: a `# Current focus` title line, a `Last updated:` line,
then exactly four `##` sections in this order, under 50 lines in total.

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>, <source>, <person or agent>

## Now

## Waiting on the owner

## Untracked to-dos

## Next session starts with
```

What the command enforces:

- It refuses a focus that lacks one of the four sections, has another
  section, or is over 50 lines (exit code 2, nothing saved).
- It adds the title line or the `Last updated:` line when either is missing,
  and sets an older date to today. It cannot know the source or who wrote
  it, so write the line yourself.

## What goes in each section

- **Last updated:** the date, the source (for example `handoff`,
  `work-finish`, `chat`), and who wrote it (a person, or `agent`). Change it
  on every save.
- **Now:** the current outcome or area, with work item ids and titles only,
  for example `- WI-012 CSV export`. Never a status or a stage: the tracker
  holds those.
- **Waiting on the owner:** a decision or action only the owner can take
  that has no work item: what it is, who needs it, and when to check again.
  Work items that wait on him are listed by `toolkit work decisions`, not
  here. A setup step (trust the hooks in Codex, sign in to Notion with
  `ntn login`) stays only while `toolkit doctor` still reports it.
- **Untracked to-dos:** things the owner asked for that have no work item.
  When one becomes a work item, replace the line with the item's id under
  Now.
- **Next session starts with:** one entry: where to resume, what to read,
  and the next action. It is replaced at each handoff, not added to.
- Write "None." in a section with nothing in it.
- Keep it under 50 lines by replacing stale lines, never by appending. Never
  drop an owner to-do that is still open only to meet the limit.

## When to check it

Check the focus before the reply ends when:

- a work item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the
  focus does not say. Check two things:
  1. Now lists the item (id and title). Add it when it is missing; take it
     off when the item is Done or Cancelled. For Done, take it off just
     before `toolkit work finish`, which backs up the focus as it is then.
  2. Next session starts with does not name a step that is done or no longer
     next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
     points at the item, for example "Continue WI-012 from its Resume here:
     build P1."
- the owner asks for something with no work item (add it under Untracked
  to-dos), or a decision only he can make has no work item (Waiting on the
  owner).
- `toolkit doctor` no longer reports a setup step listed under Waiting on the
  owner (drop it).
- a session hands off (replace the one entry under Next session starts
  with).

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. Leave every line you are
not changing exactly as it is.

## Read, change, save

1. Read it with its version. The output has `text` and `version`:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --json
   ```

2. Change only the lines that need it, in the whole text, and update the
   `Last updated:` line.
3. Save the whole text with the version you read.
   Claude Code: `<file>` is `-`, with the text on standard input after a
   quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), then a line holding only `EOF`.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
   ```

   Codex: give the text in single quotes instead (newlines are kept), or
   use a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder and delete it after the save.
   Write an apostrophe as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the
   text. Never `'\''` in Codex: the project's command rule does not match
   that form, so the command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can
   drop the backslash.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
   ```

4. Exit code 2 with "changed since it was read" means another session saved
   the focus after you read it. Read it again, make your change in the new
   text, and save with the new version. Never save without `--expect`: that
   would silently drop the other session's change.
5. No focus yet (`version` is null): save with `--expect absent`, in the full
   format above.
6. Read it back:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus
   ```

## A new project's focus

A new project's focus still holds the model's setup text: a fill-in guide
comment under the title (`<!-- Fill-in guide: ... -->`) and an
`<angle-bracket>` prompt in every section. At the first save:

- remove the fill-in guide comment;
- replace each prompt with real content, or with "None." when there is none;
- never leave an angle-bracket prompt in a saved focus.

## Examples

A full focus:

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: 2026-09-26, handoff, agent

## Now

- WI-012 CSV export
- WI-015 Large exports (sub-item of WI-012)

## Waiting on the owner

- Pick a hosting provider before the first deploy (no work item yet); check again 2026-10-01.

## Untracked to-dos

- Email the client about the October demo.

## Next session starts with

- 2026-09-26 17:40 UTC | CSV export: continue WI-012 from its Resume here. Goal: exports finish under 10 seconds.
```

The handoff entry with a work item is a pointer only:
`<UTC date and time> | <topic>: continue <WI-id> from its Resume here. Goal: <one line>.`

With no work item, the entry is a short note: the goal or topic, where work
stopped, the first next action, limits on what may be done without the
owner, and open questions. Do not create a work item only to hold it.

## Checklist for a focus save

- [ ] Read with `--json`; you have the version.
- [ ] The `# Current focus` title and the `Last updated:` line (date,
      source, who) are there.
- [ ] Four sections, in order; "None." in each empty one.
- [ ] Work item ids and titles only; no status or stage.
- [ ] No angle-bracket prompt and no fill-in guide comment left.
- [ ] Under 50 lines; no open owner to-do dropped.
- [ ] Saved with `--expect`; read back.

# Memory proposals

Purpose: what a memory proposal is, how one is saved, and how the owner's yes
or no is recorded.

## Contents

- What a proposal is
- How a proposal is saved
- Rule proposals
- Recording the owner's answer
- Examples

## What a proposal is

A proposal is a memory record the owner has not approved yet. It exists so
that a "Save to memory?" question he did not answer is kept, not lost.

- It is saved with `--proposal`: status `needs-review`, authorization
  "Proposed by the agent on <date>", and never an approver.
- It is not a fact. The agent does not rely on it, and an answer never
  presents it as true.
- `toolkit memory find` leaves it out unless `--proposals` (or `--all`) is
  given. `toolkit memory get` ends its text with a line saying it is a
  proposal.
- `toolkit work decisions` and the session briefing list it among the things
  waiting on the owner, and the `work-decide` skill asks him about it.
- The built-in index marks it "[proposal: not a fact until the owner
  answers]", or "[proposal for <concept>: ...]" when it names a concept. In
  Notion its Status is "proposed".
- A proposal never replaces a record the owner approved. The CLI refuses a
  proposal whose key is already a current or retired record.
- Concept memory: a proposal for a fact that belongs in an existing concept
  is its own record that names that concept and a section heading (its
  `concept` and `section` fields; the list shows "[proposal for <concept>:
  the owner has not answered]", and `toolkit work decisions` says "A yes adds
  it to the concept <concept>"). The concept itself does not change until his
  yes. A proposal for a new concept names none: its key is made from the
  fact's words (`project_tests_run_before_every_commit`), so on his yes you
  name the concept it goes in with `approve --concept` (below).

## How a proposal is saved

1. The agent asks the question in exactly this form, at the end of its reply:
   `Save to memory: <one-line summary>?` (bold is fine). Other wording, such
   as "Save it to memory?", has no one-line summary to save: the Stop hook
   then stops the turn once and asks for this form.
2. When the turn ends, the Stop hook reads that question. If no proposal was
   saved in this turn, the hook saves one from the summary alone. It never
   saves the same summary twice in a session. A record that is only about the
   same subject does not stop it. The next turn's context says what
   happened, in one of five notes:
   - It saved the proposal, and names its key. When the question's words
     match an existing concept of the same type, the note also says "for the
     concept <key>": his yes adds the fact there as a section. His answer is
     recorded as in "Recording the owner's answer" below.
   - It saved nothing, because memory already holds a proposal like it, and
     names that proposal. His answer approves or rejects that proposal.
   - It saved nothing, because memory already holds a record about the same
     subject, and names it. Read it with `toolkit memory get <key>`. The same
     fact in other words: keep it, or update it with `--expect <version>`. A
     different fact: after his yes, save it with `--allow-similar` and
     `--approved-by`. Never overwrite a record with a different fact.
   - It saved nothing, because the text looks like a secret. Never save it.
     After his yes, save only where the secret is kept ("The staging key is in
     1Password under Staging").
   - The save failed. Save the proposal yourself in this turn, with the
     command in step 3, so it is kept until he answers.
3. The agent may save the proposal itself in the same turn instead, with a
   full body in the record format, so the record says exactly what was
   meant. For a fact that belongs in an existing concept (the usual case),
   name the concept and the section; the text is that section's labels:

   ```text
   toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section '<heading>' --description '<the fact in one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal
   ```

   For a fact that starts a new concept:

   ```text
   toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal
   ```

`--proposal` cannot go with `--approved-by` or `--authorization`; the CLI
refuses the pair.

When a save with `--approved-by` runs in a turn whose message from the owner
held no keep phrase, no other words asking for a save, and no answer to a
memory question (the hooks record this), the CLI saves a new record or
section as a proposal instead and says so ("Saved as a proposal, not as
approved"). Then ask him, as below.

A proposal the Stop hook saved says what it came from on its Evidence and
limits line: the question as asked, and, when the owner's message that turn
stated the fact, his words ("On <date> the owner wrote "..."").

## Rule proposals

An instruction for how the agent works is a rule, not memory (the owner's
decision of 2026-09-29). When the agent inferred one, it asks "Add to the
project rules: <one line>?". An unanswered one, and a "Save to memory:
<one line>?" question whose line is such an instruction (a preference about
how work is done, a correction, a sentence that starts with a verb to the
agent), is kept as a rule proposal: a proposal typed `user` whose
`rule_section` field names the section of `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md`
it would join. The list shows "[rule proposal for .claude/rules/owner-preferences.md,
section "<area>": the owner has not answered]".

- Saving one yourself:

  ```text
  toolkit memory save --type user --name rule-<slug> --description '<the instruction in one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --rule-section '<area>' --proposal
  ```

- His yes writes the rule and removes the proposal. The instruction is the
  proposal's Remember line; `--text` gives better words, and `--section`
  another area:

  ```text
  toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>
  ```

- His no: `toolkit memory reject <key>`, as for any proposal.
- An older `feedback_` proposal is a rule proposal too: his yes writes it to
  the rules, in the section `--section` names (General when none).

## Recording the owner's answer

When you ask him about a proposal, recommend a yes only with evidence from
this project: what he said, what happened, and when. With none, ask without
a recommendation ("I have no evidence either way."). This is the one
exception to "every decision carries a recommendation" in `work-decide`.

Ask about a saved proposal as "Save to memory: <one line>?" and say it to
him: "you publish releases to npm yourself", not "Mike Rihm publishes ...".
The record keeps his name; the question speaks to him.

- **Yes, to a proposal that names a concept** (the list shows "[proposal
  for <concept> ...]"):

  ```text
  toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>
  ```

  Its fact is added to that concept, under its section heading (or under
  that heading's existing section), and the proposal record is removed; the
  output names the concept and the section.
- **Yes, to a proposal that names no concept** (a new concept, or one whose
  concept is gone): name the concept its fact goes in with `--concept`. Run
  `toolkit memory list --type <type>` first. Name an existing concept of the
  same type when the fact belongs there, or a new key named for the subject,
  never for the fact (`project_testing`, not
  `project_tests_run_before_every_commit`). A new concept also takes its
  title and its one-line summary:

  ```text
  toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner> --concept <type>_<subject> --title '<Concept title>' --description '<one-line summary of the concept>'
  ```

  The fact becomes a `## ` section of that concept, under the proposal's
  title, and the proposal record is removed. When the proposal's own key
  already names its subject, give that key to `--concept`: it is approved
  where it is. Without `--concept`, `approve` refuses such a proposal and
  lists the concepts of that type.

  Either way the concept keeps its own authorization line. When his approval
  differs from it, the section records it on its Evidence and limits line. A
  proposal the Stop hook saved ends its Evidence and limits line "so the
  toolkit's Stop hook saved it as a proposal". For that one, `approve` also
  takes the words "Do not rely on this until the owner approves it." out of
  How to apply and adds who approved it and when to the Evidence line.
- **Yes, with a reason or a detail, or the body needs work:** approve it
  first, as above, then change its section in the concept with his words
  (read the concept with `--json` for the version):

  ```text
  toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner> [--concept <type>_<subject> ...]
  toolkit memory get <concept> --json
  toolkit memory save --concept <concept> --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>
  ```

  Saving a one-fact proposal again under its own key with `--approved-by` is
  refused; a full body with `## ` sections approves it in that one save.
- **Yes, with a better name or type:** record his yes with `--concept`
  naming the better key, as above. To change a type, rename after the yes:
  `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`.
- **No:**

  ```text
  toolkit memory reject <key>
  ```

  The proposal is deleted (Notion: the Notion trash). A rejection stands:
  never propose the same fact again under other words, and never put it in
  the current focus, the glossary, or another record. When his no gives a
  general rule about what to save ("don't keep my travel plans"), write only
  that rule, with `toolkit rule add`.
- **No answer:** leave it. It stays a proposal until he answers, here or when
  `work-decide` asks.

## Examples

- The agent inferred that tests run before every commit. Reply ends with:
  "Save to memory: tests run before every commit?" The owner's next message
  is about something else. The Stop hook saved the proposal
  `project_tests_run_before_every_commit`, and it stays until `work-decide`
  asks.
- Later the owner says "yes, save that". The list of project concepts
  (`toolkit memory list --type project`) has none about testing, so the fact

  ```text
  toolkit memory approve project_tests_run_before_every_commit --by Mike --concept project_testing --title 'Testing' --description 'How and when tests run'
  ```

  Then reply with the line the output gives: "Saved to memory: tests run
  before every commit (in Testing). Say 'forget that' to undo." When
  `project_testing` exists already, the same command without `--title` and

- The owner says "no, that was only for last week". Run
  `toolkit memory reject project_tests_run_before_every_commit` and reply in

- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands, for example `save`, `retire`, `focus`, `glossary`, and `reindex` (`toolkit memory --help` lists them all). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. An instruction for how the agent works (a working preference, a correction, "from now on", "always", "never") is not memory: `memory-save` writes it to `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md` with `toolkit rule add`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, write the correction there as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those rules override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic: a new fact goes under a heading in the topic file for its concept, and a new file is only for a new concept. A lesson the agent learned and has not proven yet goes under the concept's "Gotchas and lessons" heading; when it recurs or the owner confirms it, the agent proposes it as a rule or a skill. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, or fact about the owner he stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details, a working preference or correction (a rule in `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md`) |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale (why a part of the project exists or how it is used), technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body, an instruction for how the agent works (a rule) |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode, one per file: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Saves, corrects, or retires one fact in the project's memory with `toolkit memory` commands, or sends it to its proper home. It never edits memory files by hand. Rules, skills, and memory each hold one kind of thing (Mike, 2026-09-29): an instruction the agent follows every time goes in the rules (`toolkit rule add`), a procedure that proved itself in a skill, and a fact or an unproven lesson in memory. Memory keeps one record per concept (for example `user_profile`, `project_billing`), with one `##` section per fact and a last "Gotchas and lessons" section; an `event_` record holds one episode. The prefixes are `user_`, `project_`, `reference_`, and `event_`; `feedback_` is retired.

## Steps

Track these steps in the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

1. Decide the home. An instruction for how the agent works (a preference about how work is done, a correction, "from now on", "always", "never") is a rule: save it with `toolkit rule add` ("Rules" below) and stop. A fact about why a part of the project exists or how it is used is a `project_` concept fact, even while a work item for that part is open; the item may link to it. Anything else: use the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory, which wins; otherwise `references/memory-criteria.md`). Not memory: send it to its home ("Where other things go" below) and stop.
2. Find the concept it belongs in, and any section that already holds it. List the concepts of its type (title, summary, updated date), search, and read each likely concept whole, with its version. The save's duplicate check compares wording, so only this search finds a section the new fact contradicts (for example "Mondays" against "Tuesdays").
   `toolkit memory list --type <type>`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Read the approval mode and apply "Approval policy" below. When it says ask, ask and wait.
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
4. Pick where it goes ("Choosing the concept" below), write the section text in the record format (`references/record-format.md`), and save with the form for the case ("Save forms" below).
5. Exit code 2 saved nothing. Read the "Error:" line. "Belongs in the concept <key>": add it there with the command the "Fix:" line prints, or, when it is a different concept, save again with `--new-concept`. Records listed: the duplicate check. "Changed since it was read": read it again and redo the change. Any other rule: fix the text as the message says. `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 2, has each case.
6. "Forget that" right after a section save: run the "Undo:" command the save printed (it removes that section). About a whole concept: retire it, with his words as the reason. Delete only when his own words say delete ("Approval policy").
   `toolkit memory retire <key> --reason '<his words>'`
7. An owner to-do with no work item, or a change to what is happening now: update the current focus (`references/current-focus.md`). A project term: update the glossary (`references/glossary.md`).
8. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): add the rule, then offer that change too. A lesson the agent learned itself goes under the concept's Gotchas and lessons section ("Lessons" below).
9. Read the record back, check, and reply in one line ("Replies" below). End with the question still waiting for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Approval policy

This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy.

- The owner's own words are the approval: "remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", or a correction. Save now: a fact with `--approved-by <owner>`, an instruction with `toolkit rule add`. That includes a fact about a named person he asks you to remember ("remember that Priya's last day is October 15").
- The toolkit checks this: when the hooks recorded no keep phrase, no other words asking for a save, and no answer to a memory question in his message, a save with `--approved-by` stores a new record, a new section, or added text as a proposal instead (with `--expect` too), and `toolkit rule add` stores a rule proposal instead; `toolkit rule update` and `toolkit memory promote` with `--approved-by` are refused. The output says so. Then ask him, as below.
- `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first, in exactly this form: "Save to memory: <one-line summary>?". Save after his yes (`references/proposals.md` when a proposal was saved for the question).
- A preference or fact he mentions in passing, without a keep phrase or an instruction ("screenshots were more useful than the text"), is inferred: ask "Save to memory: ...?" first. Only his keep words, or his yes to that question, are an approval.
- Recommend a yes only with evidence from this project (what he said, what happened, and when). With none, ask without a recommendation.
- `trusted` mode: a routine fact the agent is sure of is saved without asking and reported in one line, with no approver. The record says "Trusted grant".
- In either mode, always ask first for anything about a named person or personal details that he did not ask you to remember, for more than five records at once, and for a change to this policy.
- A delete needs his own words about that record ("delete it", "remove it for good"), or his yes to a numbered list that shows the delete. Do not ask again: the host asks him to confirm `toolkit memory delete`, and that prompt is the confirmation. "Forget that" is a retire, never a delete.
- A yes covers only the change and the meaning shown. Silence is never a yes.
- `--approved-by` is only for a change his words or his yes covered. Give his name exactly as the project settings hold it (`project.owner`, for example "Mike Rihm", not "Mike").
- A concept's `authorization` line is the approval of the concept. A section save never changes it; when the save's approval differs, the CLI records it on that section's Evidence and limits line (`references/record-format.md`, "Frontmatter").
- An unanswered "Save to memory?" stays a proposal until he answers (`references/proposals.md`). Never drop it, and never save it with an approver.
- Only the owner switches the mode, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Save his words as a rule in the Memory section ("Rules" below), then run one of:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`

## Choosing the concept

- One concept is one subject a future session would look up as a whole: the billing setup (`project_billing`), his role and the facts he told you about himself (`user_profile`), where dashboards live (`reference_dashboards`). How he wants the agent to work is not a concept: it is a rule.
- The fact has the concept's type. Add it to the existing concept of that type whose title and summary cover it, as a new section. The heading names the sub-topic in a few words ("Force-push", "Refund window").
- The concept already has a heading for this sub-topic: add under it with `--append`. The fact corrects what a section says: replace that section with `--expect`.
- No concept of that type covers it: start a new one. Its slug and title name the concept, not the fact (`project_billing`, not `project_invoices_go_out_on_the_1st`), and its summary says what the whole concept covers.
- An event is always its own record: one episode per `event_` record.
- Two concepts fit: pick the one a future session would open first, and link the other from the section's **Related memories** line.

## Rules

An instruction for how the agent works goes in `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md`, one `##` section per area (Replies, Questions, Testing, Git, Work items, Memory, General), each line dated with its source. `toolkit rule add` creates the file on first use and rebuilds the AGENTS.md rules list, so Codex reads it too.

- His own words are the approval. Save at once, in his words, under the area it is about. The command adds the date to the line itself:
  `toolkit rule add --section '<area>' --text '<the instruction>' --source '<owner>, in chat'`
- A memory save of an instruction he gave this turn with a keep phrase is refused (exit 2) with the `toolkit rule add` command to run instead. When it really is a fact about him or the project, not an instruction, save it again with `--not-a-rule`.
- This project is the default. When his words say every project ("in all my projects", "everywhere"), add `--machine` right after `add`; Claude Code and Codex ask him to confirm before it runs. Ask "This project or all projects?" only when his words leave it unclear.
- An instruction you inferred (he did not ask for it): ask first, in exactly this form: "Add to the project rules: <one line>?". Unanswered, the Stop hook saves it as a rule proposal. His yes writes the rule and removes the proposal (`references/proposals.md`):
  `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
- A change or removal he asked for: list the rules to see the numbers, then change or remove one:
  `toolkit rule list`
  `toolkit rule update --section '<area>' --entry <n> --text '<new words>' --source '<owner>, in chat'`
  `toolkit rule update --section '<area>' --entry <n> --remove`
- Commit what the command's Commit line names, by name. A later rule changes only `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md`: one file he asked for, which the one-file exception in `shared-repository-work.md` allows. The first rule also changes the rules list in `AGENTS.md`: two files, so commit them in your own worktree, or ask him before committing them in the shared primary checkout.
- The command prints the reply line ("Added to the project rules: ..."). Copy it.

## Lessons

A gotcha or lesson the agent learned while working, not proven yet, goes in the concept it is about, under "Gotchas and lessons", as a `###` heading with a Seen line. It needs no approval: it is the agent's own know-how, and nothing relies on it as a rule.

`toolkit memory save --concept <key> --lesson '<short heading>' --body '<what happened and what to do>' --source '<session or work item>'`

The same heading again adds today's date to its Seen line. A second session on the same day counts as its own only with its own `--source`, so always give one. When a lesson came up in two or more sessions, a lesson like it is in another concept, or the owner confirms it, propose it as a rule or a skill: `toolkit memory promote` (the `memory-tidy` skill, "Promotion").

## Save forms

`<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the body on standard input after a quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`). In Codex give `--body '<text>'` in place of `--body-file <file>`. `references/record-format.md` shows both.

The section text (`<file>`) is the labels only: no `# ` title and no `##` heading; `--section` gives the heading.

- A new fact for an existing concept, from the owner's words or his yes:
  `toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- A new concept, with its first fact:
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <concept-slug> --description '<one-line summary of the concept>' --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- In `trusted` mode, a routine fact the agent is sure of: either form without `--approved-by`.
- A question he has not answered yet: either form with `--proposal` in place of `--approved-by`. With `--concept`, `--description` is the fact in one line; the concept changes only after his yes.
- A correction of one section read in step 2, which his words or his yes covered:
  `toolkit memory save --concept <key> --section '<heading>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
- One more fact under a heading the concept already has: add `--append` to the first form.
- The concept's summary no longer covers it: add `--description '<new summary>'` to a section save.
- An event (its own record):
  `toolkit memory save --type event --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
- A whole record rewritten (rare; read it with `--json` first):
  `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
- A new record that replaces an old one: add `--supersedes <old-key>` to a new-record form.
- A better name, or a type that matches the content:
  `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script. In Codex a joined command runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight, Notion, and the main checkout's `.memory/`.
- Put one-line values (`--description`, `--source`, `--reason`) in single quotes. An apostrophe inside them: Claude Code writes `'\''`; Codex writes ’ (U+2019) or rewords, and never uses `'\''`, which runs the command inside the sandbox. Double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`, drop that text, and the save still says "Saved".
- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/memory.md`, and never write a file and run the command in one shell command.
- Body labels are bold paragraphs (`**Remember:**`), never `## Remember` headings. A `##` heading names a sub-topic; the CLI writes it from `--section`.
- A save that starts a new file for a fact whose words match an existing concept is refused with "belongs in the concept <key>". Read that concept before adding `--new-concept`.
- Replacing a section, and removing one, need `--expect <version>` from a `--json` read; adding a section does not.
- **Why** is the owner's reason in his words, or exactly "Not stated by the owner." Never a reason you inferred.
- In `onboarding` mode, a save with neither `--approved-by` nor `--proposal` is stored as "No approval recorded" (a section save: "Saved on <date> with no approval recorded." on that section's Evidence and limits line), and the save prints a "Note:" line about it. That is a mistake: fix it at once. Ask him, then save again with `--expect` and `--approved-by` after his yes, or with `--proposal` while he has not answered.
- A whole-record save of an existing key without `--expect` saves nothing. Take the version from the `--json` read; the first 12 characters are enough. Keep that read: its old text is the undo for an update.
- Add `--allow-similar` only after reading every record the duplicate check listed.
- A proposal the Stop hook saved holds only the one-line summary. His plain yes is `toolkit memory approve`, which takes out its "Do not rely on this" words. A proposal that names no concept also needs `--concept <type>_<subject>`: the concept its fact goes in, an existing one or a new key named for its subject (with `--title` and `--description`). When he adds a reason or a detail, approve it first, then save its section with his words (`references/proposals.md`).
- Never store email addresses, secrets, or work-item status. The CLI catches common secret shapes, not all. For a secret, save where it is kept, never the secret.
- A new `feedback_` record or fact is refused: the type is retired. Save the instruction with `toolkit rule add`, or the fact in a `user_` or `project_` concept.
- A memory save is not a decision for the whole project. Add to `DECISIONS.md` only when the owner asked for such a decision (`work-decide`).
- Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- Say "proposal" only for a record saved with `--proposal` (by you or the Stop hook). When nothing was saved, say that nothing was saved, and ask.
- An inferred fact whose home is a project document (for example `PROJECT.md`) is asked the same way, as one yes-or-no line: "Add to PROJECT.md: <one line>?". When he does not answer, add it to the current focus under "Waiting on the owner", so it is asked again (`references/current-focus.md`).
- The host refused `toolkit memory delete` without asking him (Codex with approvals off): the cause is that approval setting. Show him the exact command to run in a terminal and wait. Do not retire the record in its place unless he asks for that.
- Built-in memory: the CLI rebuilds `MEMORY.md` and repairs links in other notes after a rename, supersede, retire, or delete, and names each note it changed. Read that report (`references/memory-builtin.md`).

## Replies

Use these lines word for word, with the record's title, also when the memory line is one part of a longer reply. `toolkit memory save`, `approve`, and `reject` print the filled line ("Reply line for the owner, word for word"): copy it. Every memory reply ends with the next step: the question still waiting for the owner (for example "Save to memory: <one line>?"), or the exact words that continue. Never end on what was not done ("I haven't saved anything.").

- A new record or a new section: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." For a section, the title is "<heading> (in <concept title>)". His "forget that" right after a section save is the "Undo:" command the save printed.
- An update: "Updated in memory: <title>. Say 'undo that' to put back the old wording." His "undo that" is a save of the old text from the `--json` read, or of the old section text (`previous`) (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 3). Right after a supersede, the undo is a restore of the old record and a retire of the new one (same file, section 4).
- A removed section: "Removed from memory: <heading> (in <concept title>). Say 'undo that' to put it back."
- A proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."
- A rejected proposal: "Not saved: <title>. I will not suggest it again.", then the next step.
- A retire: "Retired from memory: <title>. Say 'bring it back' to restore it." His "bring it back" is the whole restore in `references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 7, not `toolkit memory restore` alone.
- A delete: "Deleted from memory, as you said: '<his words>'. This cannot be undone." For a secret or an email address, add that older backups still hold it (`references/replacing-and-retiring.md`, section 8).
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved: <reason>." Keep the text and try again later in the session. With Hindsight or Notion, the command prints the fix (`references/memory-hindsight.md`, `references/memory-notion.md`).

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds one line when the owner's message holds a keep phrase: "remember that" (or "remember this"), "from now on", "don't ever", "note that", "going forward", "keep in mind", or "Always ..." or "Never ..." at the start of a sentence. It is a reminder: route it with step 1 (an instruction to the rules, a fact to memory).
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase got no save, work-item change, or decision in the turn. Save it, or say in one line where it went instead.
- Ask in exactly the form "Save to memory: <one line>?" for a fact, or "Add to the project rules: <one line>?" for an instruction (bold is fine). Other wording, such as "Save it to memory?", makes the Stop hook stop the turn once and ask for that form.
- When a reply asks "Save to memory: <summary>?" and no proposal was saved in that turn, the Stop hook tries to save one, and the next turn's context says what happened:
  - It saved a proposal and names its key: his yes approves that key, his no rejects it (`references/proposals.md`, "Recording the owner's answer").
  - Memory already holds a proposal like it, and names it: his answer approves or rejects that proposal.
  - It saved a proposal for an existing concept ("for the concept <key>"): his yes adds the fact to that concept as a section.
  - It saved a rule proposal (an instruction for how the agent works, or the "Add to the project rules" form): his yes, `toolkit memory approve` with the key, adds it to `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md`; `--section '<area>'` names another section.
  - Memory already holds a record about the same subject, and names it: read it as in step 2. The same fact: keep it, or update it with `--expect`. A different fact and his yes: add it to that concept as a section, or save it with `--allow-similar` and `--approved-by`. Never overwrite a record with a different fact.
  - The text looks like a secret, so nothing was saved: never save it; after his yes, save only where the secret is kept.

### Starting request

I want the late fee command built. When I run node bin/feecalc.js 200 --days 10 it should print "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00". The fee is 0.25% of the invoice amount for each day late. I also want a --cents option that adds a second line with the total due in whole cents, like "Total due in cents: 20500", because that is what our billing API takes. Do not build anything until I approve the requirements.

### Agreed goal

Provide a command that calculates a 0.25% daily late fee on an invoice and prints the late fee and total due in dollars. WI-002 delivers the separately requested --cents option under R-03.

### Active requirements

#### R-01 — Calculate the late fee

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** An overdue invoice amount and the number of days late supplied to the command.  
**Required behavior:** Calculate the late fee as 0.25% of the original invoice amount for each day late. Round the fee to the nearest cent, with half a cent rounded up. The total due is the invoice amount plus that rounded fee.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Valid invoice amounts are $0 or more with at most two decimal places. Valid day counts are whole numbers of 0 or more. Missing or invalid inputs do not produce a calculated total.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the fee is $5.00 and the total due is $205.00. For an invoice amount of $1 and 2 days late, the half-cent fee rounds up to $0.01 and the total due is $1.01. A missing or invalid amount or day count produces no calculated total.  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, rounding answer, input rule answer, missing or invalid input answer, total due answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

#### R-02 — Print the dollar amounts

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** A command run with an invoice amount and the days-late option.  
**Required behavior:** For valid input, print one line containing the late fee and total due in dollars, each with two decimal places. For missing or invalid input, print a clear error to standard error, exit unsuccessfully, and print no total.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** No second line is requested unless the cents option is supplied.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the first line is exactly "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00". A run with a missing or invalid input prints a clear error on standard error, exits unsuccessfully, and prints no total.  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, missing or invalid input answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

#### R-03 — Print total due in cents on request

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** A command run with the cents option.  
**Required behavior:** Add a second line with the total due as a whole number of cents for the billing API.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** The cents value must represent the invoice amount plus the rounded fee, matching the total due shown in dollars.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the cents option adds the line "Total due in cents: 20500" after the dollar line. For an invoice amount of $1 and 2 days late, it adds "Total due in cents: 101".  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, rounding answer, total due answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

This work item can be accepted when:

1. Running node bin/feecalc.js 200 --days 10 prints exactly "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00" (R-01, R-02).
2. Running the command with a missing or invalid input prints a clear error on standard error, exits unsuccessfully, and prints no total (R-01, R-02).
